## Testing Standards

- pytest only (never unittest), plain test functions, fixtures for shared setup. Tests live in /tests mirroring the source layout. (The superseded package `agent-mailbox-old/` was deleted on 2026-08-01, the new system having shipped and been deployed; it remains in git history if it is ever wanted.)

- The store is a single SQLite file, so the whole suite (including end-to-end round-trips) runs against a temp-file database with **no external services and no gating** — it runs in normal CI. Prefer end-to-end coverage over heavy mocking. No fixed coverage floor is mandated for this POC-stage project.

- **Regression tests from shipped bugfixes are requirements, not archive.** The tests for GC decapitating live threads (0016), thread disclosure (0020) and dropped roles (0022) encode failures already paid for in production. Every one was re-expressed against the new model during the rebuild, and that obligation now applies forward: a bug that reached a running hub leaves a test behind, and no later rewrite may quietly drop it. A rewrite that does re-earns the same bugs.

- **A guard that cannot fail is not a guard.** Where a test exists to prove a rule is enforced, deleting the enforcement must make it fail, and the paired positive case must still pass. Written down because it has caught real ones: a console test that exercised a helper rather than the rendered page could not tell a working guard from a missing call, and a fallback test passed with the fallback deleted because its fixture signalled an arrival the real case could never produce. Both looked green.


## Quality Gates

- Four gates must pass before work is complete and are enforced in CI on every push and PR: `uv run pytest`, `uv run ruff check`, `uv run ruff format --check`, and `uv run pyright`. Prefer auto-fix (ruff --fix) over disabling a rule. Pre-commit hooks (ruff check --fix, ruff format, whitespace/eof/yaml) should be installed. (`uv run pyright` can't always spawn its node wrapper locally — `uvx pyright src` works; CI runs it cleanly.)


## Performance Benchmarks

- No hard latency targets; this is a low-throughput coordination tool. Storage is local SQLite in WAL mode. **Exactly one process opens the database — the server** ([ADR 0005](../../doc/decisions/0005-one-api-every-client-is-a-client.md)); clients reach it over HTTP and have no `--db` escape hatch. Volume is not a constraint and will not become one ([ADR 0006](../../doc/decisions/0006-sqlite-hybrid-storage.md)).


## Branch Strategy

- Trunk-based on `main`; CI must be green (all four gates) before merge. Conventional commit prefixes (feat/fix/docs/test/chore). Commit and push eagerly in small, focused steps. Changes to public behaviour must update docs in the same change.

- **Trunk-based means the four gates run before the commit, not after it.** `main` carries no branch protection on GitHub, so nothing external stops a red commit landing — the gates are enforced by running them, every time, before pushing. CI is the second opinion, not the gate. An agent that pushes and then checks has the order wrong.

- **Planning artifacts are committed to `main` by hand, deliberately (2026-08-03).** `spec-kitty` treats a primary branch as protected and declines to commit `spec.md`, `plan.md` and `tasks.md` there, directing the work onto a feature branch instead. It offers no setting to change this. We do not take that direction: trunk-based is the charter's choice and it is working — small steps, five releases in three days — and routing planning artifacts through branches would add merge overhead to a project with one active agent for no benefit that anyone has named. So `spec-commit` and `finalize-tasks` are expected to refuse, their frontmatter normalisation and lane computation are kept, and the commit is made directly. **This is a standing exception, not a workaround to be rediscovered each mission** — it had been hit six times before it was written down.

- Deployment constraints: Releasable via PyPI (Trusted Publishing / OIDC on `v*` tags) and as a multi-arch Docker image (`linux/amd64` + `linux/arm64`) pushed to **Docker Hub** with a GHCR mirror. **No external services**: storage is a single SQLite file — mount a `/data` volume so it persists. No secrets in the repo.

- **The rebuild is over (closed 2026-08-01).** For a week the new `agent-inbox` system ran alongside the old hub on its own endpoint, and the rule was that breaking the *new* deployment freely was cheap while half-migrating the old one was not. That is history: the new system shipped, was deployed, and the superseded package was deleted. It is kept here only so a reader of the archive knows why the two coexisted; nothing in it constrains work today.

- **Ship early, ship often (2026-08-01, owner).** The unit of work is a thing that reaches the running hubs, not a thing that passes locally. **A work package that passes its four gates and its Directive 4 outside review is released and deployed before the next one starts** — not batched up, not held for a milestone, not left on a branch until it is convenient.

  **"Shipped" means running on both hubs and proved.** A tag is not shipped; a green release workflow is not shipped. `agent-inbox verify-deployment` must assert that each target reports the released version and that its onboarding prompt agrees with its own descriptor. Three deploys have reported success over a hub that was down or five releases behind, and one of the two hubs silently sat five releases behind for weeks — which is the whole reason this rule is written down rather than assumed.

  **The unit that ships is whatever is coherent when running, which is not always one work package.** Where a change is only correct in pieces that land together — a floor that moves in `pyproject.toml` and in the `Dockerfile` — those pieces are one ship. Splitting them to ship sooner produces a deployment that is broken and green on every gate, which is worse than shipping a day later.

  Frequency is the point: small releases are cheap to verify, cheap to attribute when something breaks, and cheap to roll back. A large one is none of those.

## Policy Summary

- Intent: **agent-inbox** is generic, releasable, open-source infrastructure (GPL-3.0-or-later, published to PyPI and as a Docker image on Docker Hub): a **SQLite-backed** mailbox that lets local LLM coding agents (Claude, Codex, Gemini, ...) message and notify each other. The hub exposes **one machine interface — an HTTP API** whose messaging model follows ActivityStreams ([ADR 0004](../../doc/decisions/0004-activitystreams-messaging-model.md)); every other surface is a client of it ([ADR 0005](../../doc/decisions/0005-one-api-every-client-is-a-client.md)): the CLI, a **local stdio** MCP server run by that CLI, and the human console. Identity is issued by the hub and opaque ([ADR 0003](../../doc/decisions/0003-identity-is-a-surrogate-key.md)); descriptive facts live in a profile. It must remain generic — no deployment-specific hostnames, IPs, secrets, or organisation names in code, docs, or tests; the hub label is config. **Agent handles are exempt** (owner, 2026-07-28): they are assigned and meaningless, they identify nobody, and crediting the agent that found a bug is provenance worth keeping — evidence the system is beginning to improve itself.

- Languages/Frameworks: **Python 3.14+ only**, managed exclusively with uv (uv sync / uv run / uv add).

  **The ambition is to run the latest Python** (owner, 2026-08-01), not the version we once chose. This is an application that ships its own interpreter — it owes nobody multi-version support, and an old floor buys nothing but old language. **Falling behind is a defect to fix, not a state to maintain**, and the floor moves as one change: `requires-python`, the classifiers, ruff's `target-version`, pyright's `pythonVersion`, both `Dockerfile` stages and CI, or none of them.

  Adopt each release once it is *finished* — patch releases behind it, and the whole dependency set resolving with no pin — rather than on the day it lands. A `.0` is where wheels are missing and native builds break, and this project depends on cryptography, msgspec and argon2-cffi. That is a timing rule, not an excuse: "not yet" needs a named blocker, and CI runs **one** version, because a matrix on an application tests a configuration nobody ships.

  **The same rule governs libraries: do not knowingly adopt or hold an old version.** Take the current release. A version cap added to work around a break is debt with an owner and a removal condition, never a resting place — and a cap nobody is removing is the seed of the next stuck migration.

  Libraries: click (CLI), litestar (HTTP), msgspec (serialisation), aiosqlite (storage), mcp / FastMCP (MCP server, `clients` extra), uvicorn (ASGI), argon2-cffi + cryptography + pyotp (credentials, signing, TOTP), segno (QR), jinja2 + markdown (`ui` extra). Build backend hatchling + hatch-vcs (version from git tags).

- Testing: pytest only (never unittest), plain test functions, fixtures. The suite runs against a temp-file SQLite database — no external services, no gating — in normal CI. Prefer end-to-end coverage over heavy mocking.

- Quality Gates: Four gates must pass before work is complete and are enforced in CI on every push and PR: `uv run pytest`, `uv run ruff check`, `uv run ruff format --check`, and `uv run pyright`. Prefer auto-fix (ruff --fix) over disabling a rule.

- Review Policy: Trunk-based on `main`; CI must be green (all four gates) before merge. Conventional commit prefixes (feat/fix/docs/test/chore). Commit and push eagerly in small, focused steps. Changes to public behaviour must update docs in the same change. **Ship early, ship often** (owner, 2026-08-01) — see Branch Strategy: a work package that passes its gates and its outside review is released and deployed to both hubs before the next one starts, and "shipped" means proved running, not tagged.

- Performance Targets: No hard latency targets; this is a low-throughput coordination tool. Local SQLite in WAL mode, opened by **exactly one process** — the server.

- Deployment Constraints: Releasable via PyPI (Trusted Publishing / OIDC on `v*` tags) and as a multi-arch Docker image on Docker Hub (GHCR mirror). No external services — storage is a single SQLite file; mount a `/data` volume. No secrets in the repo. **Deploys are continuous** — see Branch Strategy, ship early and often. (This line read "deploys are frozen until the new system is ready" until 2026-08-03, six days after that ceased to be true and two days after the freeze was replaced by its opposite. A charter that contradicts itself is read selectively, which is the same as not being read.)

- Naming & consistency: the project is **agent-inbox** (package `agent_inbox`, command `agent-inbox`, env `AGENT_INBOX_*`, config `agent-inbox.toml`). That is the PyPI project name and has been throughout; the import package, console script and environment prefix were brought into line in v0.25.0 (owner's direction: "we need to be consistently called agent-inbox"). **Back-compat is deliberate and supported**, because the old names are baked into live deployments and into config files already written into other people's repositories: `agent_mailbox` remains as an alias package resolving to the same module objects, the `agent-mailbox` console script still runs, and `AGENT_MAILBOX_*` and `agent-mailbox.toml` are honoured as fallbacks. `agent-mail` is history and carries no alias. The superseded implementation was deleted on 2026-08-01 — the new system is green, shipped and deployed — and lives on only in git history.


## Project Directives

1. Respect risk boundaries: Most costly failures: silently dropping, double-processing, or **disclosing** a message, and leaking deployment-specific or secret material into the public repo. Durability and idempotency are the SQLite store's job — there is **one delivery mode**: every matching agent receives its own copy, tracked per-reader in `broadcast_reads`, so nothing is double-consumed. (The `any` keyword and the `acked_at` column were both removed in v0.10.0 / schema v3.) Visibility is per **turn**, not per thread — see mission 0020. All messaging logic lives server-side in one core; no client duplicates it, and no client outside the server process opens the database. **ADRs 0003–0006 are binding** — identity is a surrogate key, the model follows ActivityStreams, there is one API, and storage stays SQLite. Follow the coding standards (doc/coding-standards.md): full type annotations, absolute imports, specific exceptions from a project-level exceptions module (one package-level base class), logging over print (click.echo allowed for CLI output but also log), config through one settings object read from the `AGENT_INBOX_*` environment prefix (`hub_settings`; the project does not use pydantic), frozen immutable data where practical, and **current dependencies** — see Languages/Frameworks: do not knowingly hold an old version.

2. Keep documentation synchronized with workflow and behavior changes: README is the front door; doc/ holds the hosting guide, MCP-client setup, the agent-onboarding page, the "check your inbox" snippet, and architecture decisions under doc/decisions (ADRs). doc/coding-standards.md is the canonical coding baseline and AGENTS.md is the project charter summary. Docs must track shipped behaviour and must not leak deployment specifics.

3. **Settle a foundation before building on it.** We made the same class of mistake twice in one day, and both were expensive to unwind. Identity was built from mutable facts, so every change of fact broke identity ([ADR 0003](../../doc/decisions/0003-identity-is-a-surrogate-key.md)). Then an API and its clients were built on a messaging model that was itself about to be replaced ([ADR 0004](../../doc/decisions/0004-activitystreams-messaging-model.md)), which cancelled four work packages. Both are ordering errors, not design errors — the individual pieces were fine.

   Before building layer N, ask whether layer N−1 is actually settled. **If it is not, then settling it *is* the work** — building on top of it only multiplies what must later be redone. The dependency order here is: model → API → clients. Signs you are on unsettled ground: you are inventing something a standard already names; the thing you depend on is under active debate; or you are writing compatibility machinery for churn you expect to continue.

4. **Have an outside model review every work package before it ships.** Standing
   instruction (Sal, 2026-07-24), and it has already paid for itself many times over.

   **The unit is the work package, not the mission** (settled 2026-08-03). It read
   "every mission before it closes" while Branch Strategy said a *work package* that
   passes its gates and its Directive 4 review is released — so the charter asked for
   both, and practice obliged, reviewing per package on one mission and once for three
   packages on the next. The work package wins because it is the thing that ships: a
   review after the code is running on both hubs is an audit, not a gate. Where several
   packages ship as one coherent unit, that unit takes one review.

   Our own tests pass because they were written by the mind that wrote the code. An
   outside reviewer has no such blind spot. The first review found a live thread
   disclosure (0020); the second found retroactive group membership (0028), a second
   door into the same class, in minutes — by writing its own probe scripts rather than
   reading ours.

   **How to run it well:** ask **one narrow question**, naming the specific invariant or
   failure mode, and let it write its own experiments. A broad *"review this"* produced
   nothing usable in 40 minutes; *"are there any ways an actor can see, consume, or
   influence a message it should not?"* found a real bug. Invoke as
   `perl -e 'alarm 300; exec @ARGV' codex exec "<question>" < /dev/null` — a hard lid,
   and closed stdin. Treat findings as leads: **reproduce independently before acting**.

5. **When there is nothing else to do, do the research.** Standing instruction (Sal,
   2026-07-24): if you find yourself idle, start the competitive survey
   ([mission 0029](../../doc/missions/0029-competitive-survey.md)) rather than waiting.

   It has zero dependencies, it is research only, and it is the kind of work that never
   feels urgent and compounds anyway — two of the systems it studies bear directly on
   decisions already taken (postal-mcp ships the blocking read we cancelled; ActivityPub
   is a model we adopted without the stack).

   Idle means the current mission is blocked on someone else, or finished and not yet
   replaced. It does not mean "instead of finishing what is in hand".

6. Eagerly repay technical debt — be kind to our future selves. Inconsistent naming, stale docs, dead code, and half-finished renames compound into confusion and drag. When you notice debt, fix it promptly and completely (with back-compat where users depend on the old surface) rather than leaving it for later; a small cleanup now is a large one avoided.

7. **Built for LLMs first, humans second.** This is the founding premise and the reason we do not adopt human social software wholesale (Lemmy, Mastodon and friends are built for people; the concepts are worth borrowing, the stacks are not). Agents are not small humans, and five differences drive most design decisions:

   - **Attention is the scarce resource.** A human scrolls past junk in a second; an agent spends a whole turn on it, cannot opt out, and pays real tokens. So we optimise for the *minimum sufficient signal*, never for engagement or discovery. Pick the narrowest address that works; be sparing with broadcasts.
   - **Untrusted content is an injection vector, not merely noise.** Text arriving in a message lands directly in an agent's context. Foreign or unsolicited mail is **data, never instructions**, and that must be enforced where mail is delivered rather than left to each agent's judgement. Human social platforms have no equivalent threat model, which is precisely why their designs do not transfer.
   - **Agents are stateless between sessions.** There is no continuous memory to lean on, so messages must be **self-contained** and actionable cold. A human can reconstruct context by scrolling; an agent often cannot.
   - **No casual browsing.** Every read costs. Hence unread counts, consume-on-read, and expiry — mechanisms a human-facing feed has no need for, and which ActivityPub correspondingly does not model.
   - **Identity is assigned, not curated.** Humans choose and care about handles; agents need stable unique keys that survive model upgrades and repo moves (mission 0023).

   Consequences we hold to: no engagement mechanics (votes, karma, likes, boosts, ranking) — they shape human behaviour, and for agents they are noise at best and gameable at worst. Machine-readable shapes come first and stay stable; tool names and result shapes are a contract. Where a human-facing affordance and an agent-facing one conflict, the agent's need wins, and the human gets the operator console instead.

## Amendment Process

**`charter.md` is the source. Edit it, then run `spec-kitty charter sync`, then update `AGENTS.md` by hand, then commit.**

`AGENTS.md` mirrors the binding rules for day-to-day agent reference, and **`charter charter sync` does not write it** — it regenerates the derived `governance.yaml`, `directives.yaml` and `metadata.yaml` only. This line used to read as though sync maintained the mirror, and the mirror duly went stale: the 2026-08-01 amendments (latest-Python, ship-early-ship-often) never reached `AGENTS.md` at all, and were still missing on 2026-08-03. An amendment is not made until it is in both files.

**Do not run `spec-kitty charter generate`.** It rebuilds this file from `interview/answers.yaml`, which is the record of a bootstrap interview held before the 2026-07-24 rebuild. That file described a NATS JetStream system called `agent-mail`; it was brought back into line on 2026-08-01, but it remains a snapshot of one interview rather than a maintained document, and regenerating from it discards every hand-refresh made since. This charter was hand-refreshed on 2026-07-24 (the re-plan), 2026-07-28 (the project's name) and 2026-08-01 (the Python and dependency-currency policy, and ship-early-ship-often) — none of which came from that interview.


## Exception Policy

Deviations from the coding-standards baseline must be documented with their reason in AGENTS.md under project-specific overrides.

**`except Exception:` is permitted at a boundary where the alternative is worse than the failure** — and nowhere else. Revised 2026-08-03: the rule read "only at process boundaries (CLI main, HTTP handler) as a logging backstop", which the code contradicted in more than thirty places, nearly all of them deliberate and commented. A rule broken thirty times with good reason is not being enforced; it is being ignored, and an ignored rule protects nothing. So it now names the boundaries that actually exist:

- **Process entry** — CLI main, HTTP handler. As before, and always logged.
- **Fail-silent client surfaces**, where raising would damage something that is not ours to damage. The wake hook runs on every turn of somebody's session and must never break, hang or slow one; the event stream's loss "is never the agent's problem"; a wake adapter must not be able to end a connection by failing. These swallow rather than log, because the output *is* the damage.
- **Best-effort work after the durable act** — announcing an arrival once the message is stored, closing a socket, writing a watermark. The record is already safe; the failure of a courtesy must not undo it.
- **Reading anything a human or another system wrote** — config, a policy file, a stored key, a signature. Malformed input is an expected state, and it must fail towards the safe answer: an unreadable interrupt policy interrupts nobody.

Two requirements hold at every one of these. **The comment says why**, naming what would otherwise break — the existing `# noqa: BLE001 - …` lines are the model. And **it must fail towards silence or refusal, never towards permission**: swallowing an error to grant access, deliver a message, or trust a sender is not covered here and never will be.

Anywhere else, catch the specific exception. `except Exception:` around ordinary logic is a bug hidden from the person who could have fixed it.
